Revulsion

rih-VUL-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Revulsion is a strong feeling of disgust or repulsion.

The jury's faces showed open revulsion as the prosecutor described the crime scene in detail.

Worked Example

Watching the documentary about the polluted river, viewers reported feeling genuine revulsion at the sight of dead fish floating for miles downstream.

Revulsion is more than dislike -- it's a strong, almost physical reaction of disgust.

How Revulsion Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disgust

disgust: a strong feeling of dislike or repulsion

repulsion

repulsion: a strong feeling of being pushed away by something unpleasant

Antonyms

attraction

attraction: a strong feeling of being drawn toward something

delight

delight: a feeling of great pleasure

How Strong Is It? — distaste → revulsion → horror

distaste vs. revulsion

distaste vs. revulsion: Distaste is only a mild dislike, far less intense than genuine disgust.

horror vs. revulsion

horror vs. revulsion: Horror is an even more extreme reaction, often mixed with fear, beyond ordinary disgust.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, away (Latin)

root — vuls-

root — vuls-: to pull, to tear (from Latin vellere, whose past stem is vuls-)

suffix — -ion

suffix — -ion: the act or state of; forms a noun (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Revulsion is built from re- ('back, away') + vuls- ('to pull, to tear,' from Latin vellere, whose past stem is vuls-) + -ion (a noun ending) -- literally a sudden 'pulling back' or 'tearing away,' which captures exactly how your body reacts when something disgusts you.

Use the root in a new word: convulsion

Use the root in a new word: convulsion: The patient's muscles shook with a brief convulsion before the medication finally took effect.
